unit.title: Perform manual metal arc welding process to AWS specification (Low carbon steel sheet)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which job is most likely to be welded to a sheet steel procedure, and not to a structural plate procedure?
options: Splicing the 20 mm flanges of a bridge beam
Welding a 25 mm base plate to a column
Fixing 1.5 mm cold-formed purlins to cleats
Joining 12 mm plates for a tank floor

questions.stem: The WPS for a sheet job gives 55–75 A for a 2.5 mm E6013 electrode. A welder keeps burning holes at 75 A. What should he do first?
options: Work lower in the range and travel a bit faster
Change to a 4.0 mm electrode at the same current
Turn the current up so the holes fill faster
Weave wider and slower to spread the heat out

questions.stem: Why does a sheet steel WPS (welding procedure specification) state the range of sheet thickness it covers?
options: The thickness sets the price of the electrodes used
Sheet steel is only made in one standard thickness
The code does not allow sheets of mixed thickness
Settings for thick sheet can burn through thin sheet

questions.stem: A drawing note calls for welding to the sheet steel code the Centre uses and its WPS. Marlon has only passed a test on 10 mm plate. What should the team leader do?
options: Let him weld, as plate is harder to weld than sheet
Check his test covers sheet, or test him on sheet
Let him weld, but only with a larger electrode
Let him weld, but only in the flat position

questions.stem: Steel roof deck sheet is galvanised (zinc coated). Before arc spot welding it, what is the main extra control?
options: Wet the deck so the zinc stays cool while welding
Fume extraction or suitable respiratory protection
Weld only at night, when the air is cooler
Cover the deck with a fire blanket while welding

questions.stem: Why is arc welding on a steel sheet roof deck a special hazard for the welder?
options: The sheet reflects too little arc light to see the joint
Electrodes cannot be kept dry while up on a roof
The deck makes the welding machine overheat
Falls from height, and metal all round in the circuit

questions.stem: Thin sheet gets hot very quickly. What is the safe way to handle a sheet panel that has just been welded?
options: Use tongs or heat-resistant gloves, and mark it HOT
Pick it up quickly by the corners with bare hands
Slide it off the bench so it drops to the floor to cool
Leave it in the walkway where others can see it

questions.stem: A welder must arc weld a sheet metal duct in the ceiling space above an office in Kingston. What is needed before work starts?
options: Only a bucket of water placed at the foot of the ladder
A note asking office staff to close their windows
A hot work permit, fire watch and checks above and below
A larger electrode, so that the job finishes sooner

questions.stem: Which electrode diameter is usually the best choice for MMAW of 1.6 mm low carbon steel sheet?
options: 5.0 mm
4.0 mm
3.2 mm
2.0 mm

questions.stem: Why is an E6013 (rutile) electrode often chosen for welding thin low carbon steel sheet?
options: It gives the deepest penetration of the common electrodes
Its soft arc and shallow penetration suit thin sheet
It needs no current setting on the welding machine
It is the only kind of electrode that runs on AC

questions.stem: The maker says an electrode may be run on DC electrode negative (DCEN). Why might a welder choose DCEN for thin sheet?
options: It makes the slag much easier to chip off
It doubles the deposit rate of the electrode
It puts less heat into the sheet
It removes the need for any fume control

questions.stem: Why is a short, steady arc length especially important when welding thin sheet?
options: A long arc wanders and is hard to control
A short arc uses much less electricity from the supply
A long arc makes the slag too hard to chip off
A short arc stops the flux coating from melting

questions.stem: On a lap joint in 2 mm sheet, why must the welder not melt away the top edge of the upper sheet?
options: It reduces the throat, so the weld is weaker
It changes the colour of the finished bead
It makes the slag stick harder to the joint
It only matters when welding on AC current

questions.stem: A flare-bevel groove weld is often called for on cold-formed sheet sections. Where is this weld made?
options: Between two flat sheet edges that are cut square
Inside a hole punched through the top sheet first
Where a rounded bent corner meets a flat face
Across the end of a sheet that is folded back on itself

questions.stem: What is an arc spot weld (sometimes called a puddle weld) on steel deck?
options: A short tack used only to hold sheets before seam welding
A round weld through the top sheet, with no hole first
A weld made inside a hole drilled through both sheets first
A row of small spots made with a resistance spot welder

questions.stem: When the deck sheet is very thin, the WPS may call for a weld washer at each arc spot weld. What is the washer for?
options: To connect the deck back to the welding machine
To mark where each spot weld must be made
To stop the electrode sticking to the deck
To stop the thin sheet burning away round the weld

questions.stem: Two 1.6 mm sheets are to be joined with a square butt weld. Which fit-up is best?
options: A gap of about 5 mm, so the weld can get right through
A 30° bevel on each edge, as used on thick plate
Clean edges set close together and tacked often
Edges overlapped by 10 mm and tacked at the ends

questions.stem: Why are tack welds placed closer together on thin sheet than on thick plate?
options: Sheet steel needs far more weld metal to be strong
Close tacks let the welder use a bigger electrode
Short tack spacing is a rule of the electrode maker
Thin sheet moves easily with heat

questions.stem: Which method best controls distortion when welding a 1 m seam in 2 mm sheet?
options: Clamp it over a backing bar and weld short, spaced runs
Weld the whole seam in one slow, wide weaving run
Weld the seam with the largest electrode in the store
Heat the whole sheet red hot before welding starts

questions.stem: A copper backing bar is clamped under a butt joint in sheet. What does it do?
options: It is welded in and becomes part of the finished joint
It draws heat away and supports the root
It adds copper to the weld to make it stronger
It takes the place of the work lead and clamp

questions.stem: A WPS for thin sheet may allow vertical-down welding. Why?
options: It gives deeper penetration than welding upward
Quicker travel means less heat goes into the sheet
Vertical-down needs no change of electrode angle
The slag runs ahead of the pool and protects it

questions.stem: When fillet welding thin sheet to a thicker section, where should the arc mainly be aimed?
options: At the thicker part, so the pool washes onto it
At the thin sheet, since it melts more slowly
Down the middle, with no change for the thickness
Away from both parts, so the heat spreads out

questions.stem: While welding a lap joint overhead (4F) in sheet, the pool sags and drips. Which change helps most?
options: A longer arc and a slower travel speed
A larger electrode and more current
A wide weave to spread the metal out
Less current and small, quick runs

questions.stem: In a horizontal (2F) lap joint, the top edge of the upper sheet keeps melting back. What is the most likely cause?
options: The electrode is too small for the joint
The travel speed is too fast
The arc is aimed too much at the top edge
The sheet was cleaned too well

questions.stem: Why should the crater at the end of each weld run on sheet be filled before the arc is broken?
options: So the electrode lasts a little longer
So the slag is easier to chip
So the stub is used up fully
An open crater can crack

questions.stem: A drawing shows an intermittent fillet weld marked "50-150" on a sheet panel. What does this mean?
options: A 50 mm leg size, 150 mm long in total
50 separate welds, each 150 mm long
Welds 50 mm long, spaced at 150 mm centres
Welds 150 mm long with 50 mm gaps between

questions.stem: A 1.5 mm sheet is to be fillet welded to a 3 mm sheet. Which thickness normally guides the current setting?
options: The thicker sheet, so the weld fuses fully into it
The thinner sheet, taking care to fuse the thicker one
The average of the two thicknesses added together
Neither, as the current depends only on the position

questions.stem: What does "low carbon steel" (mild steel) mean for the welder?
options: It welds easily, with little risk of it cracking
It must always be preheated to a high temperature
It can only be welded with a stainless electrode
It can only be joined by oxy-acetylene welding

questions.stem: Sheet arrives with mill oil on its surface. Why must the oil be cleaned off before welding?
options: Oil gives off gas in the arc, causing porosity
Oil makes the sheet too soft to cut cleanly
Oil changes the real thickness of the sheet
Oil makes the electrode coating fall off

questions.stem: A delivery note says the sheet is "16 gauge". What should the welder do before setting up?
options: Treat it as 16 mm thick and set the current to suit
Measure the real thickness in millimetres with a caliper
Set the highest current, as gauge sheet is always thick
Use the gauge number as the current in amps

questions.stem: Under a sheet WPS, which visual fault is most likely to be rejected straight away?
options: Light spatter beside the weld
Slight colour change beside the weld
A crack at the end of the weld
Small, even ripples on the bead

questions.stem: Two lapped sheets joined by arc spot welds are pried or twisted apart to check the welds. What is this test usually called?
options: A hardness test
A tensile test
A macro test
A peel test

questions.stem: When arc spot welds are pulled apart in a test, which result shows a good weld?
options: The sheets part cleanly, with no metal torn
The weld splits through its middle, leaving a shiny face
A button of weld pulls out, tearing a hole in the sheet
The sheets stay flat and do not bend at all

questions.stem: Why is a sheet bend test strip bent round a former (mandrel) of a set size, and not just folded flat?
options: So every strip is bent the same way
So the strip cannot break during the test
Because thin sheet cannot be bent by hand
So that the weld face is hidden inside the bend

questions.stem: A sheet butt weld has holes burnt through it every 100 mm or so. What is the likely cause?
options: Current too low and electrode too small
Too much heat where the welder paused or slowed
The sheet was cleaned too well before welding
The electrodes had been kept too dry

questions.stem: Besides the welds themselves, which check matters most on a welded sheet panel?
options: The colour of the primer on the panel
The weight of the electrodes left over
The time taken for each weld run
Flatness and sizes against the drawing

questions.stem: What is a welder performance qualification record (WPQ) used for?
options: To list the prices the shop charges for welding
To record the welding machine's service history
To show that the procedure (WPS) has been tested
To show what a welder has passed

questions.stem: What is a procedure qualification record (PQR)?
options: A list of the welders who have passed their tests
The record of test welds that prove a WPS works
A drawing that shows each weld with its own number
A daily log of the electrode oven temperature

questions.stem: A qualified welder has not used MMAW for many months. What does the AWS code the Centre uses generally say about his qualification?
options: It may lapse, so a retest may then be needed
It lasts for life once it has been passed
It carries over to any other welding process
It lapses only if the machine is changed

questions.stem: Which change on a sheet job would most likely need a new or re-tested WPS?
options: A new box of the same electrode from the same maker
A different welder who is qualified for the work
Changing to an electrode of a different AWS class
Moving the bench to the other side of the shop

questions.stem: You lead three welders on 40 sheet steel cabinets for a hotel in Negril. What should happen before the first cabinet is fully welded?
options: Check only that enough electrodes are in stock
Weld and check a trial piece to the WPS
Let each welder use the settings he likes best
Paint the cabinets so the welds will be hidden

questions.stem: Why should the electrode class, size and current used on each batch of sheet panels be written down?
options: So the welders can be paid by the hour
So the machine maker can renew its warranty
So a fault found later can be traced and put right
So the electrode store can close early

questions.stem: A trainee's sheet welds are full of burn-through holes. He says he is copying the settings he used on plate. What is the best coaching?
options: Tell him to weld faster without changing anything else
Move him to plate work and give the sheet to another welder
Tell him to fill each hole with extra weld metal
Show him the sheet WPS range and let him practise on scrap

questions.stem: A 1.8 m seam is welded with stitch welds 50 mm long at 150 mm centres. About how many stitch welds are there?
Thin offcuts with sharp edges are left after a sheet job. Where should they go?
options: Leave them on the floor for the cleaner
Throw them in the general waste bin
Put them in the scrap bin
Stack them on the welding bench for next time

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the weld made through the top sheet of a deck into the steel below, with no hole made first?
What is the name of the fault where the arc melts right through thin sheet and leaves a hole?
What is the name of the joint where two sheets overlap and are fillet welded along an edge?
What is the name of the thin steel ring placed on very thin deck before an arc spot weld, so the sheet does not burn away?
A lap joint test piece in sheet is welded with the welder working from below the joint. What is the AWS position code for this fillet weld?
An intermittent fillet weld is marked 40-120. How long is the gap, in mm, from the end of one weld to the start of the next?
What is the name of the groove weld made where the rounded corner of a bent sheet section meets a flat surface?
What do the letters PQR stand for in welding procedure work?
With an electrode that allows both, which DC polarity puts less heat into thin sheet: DCEP or DCEN?
A panel has 6 stitch welds, each 40 mm long, on each of its 4 sides. What is the total length of weld, in mm?
What illness, with flu-like shivers and fever, can be caused by breathing zinc fume when welding galvanised sheet?
What is the name for distortion where a thin welded panel bulges and pops in and out when pressed, like the lid of a tin?
What is the AWS position code for a butt (groove) weld in sheet held upright, with the weld running vertically?
What is the name of the plan that sets the order and direction of the welds on a panel to keep distortion down?
A sheet is 1.5 mm thick. The WPS allows a root gap of no more than half the sheet thickness. What is the largest gap allowed, in mm?

essays.stem: Explain what makes MMAW of low carbon steel sheet harder than MMAW of plate, and how a sheet steel WPS deals with each problem.
essays.modelAnswer: Thin sheet holds little heat, so the arc can burn straight through it. It also moves and buckles as it heats and cools, and the edges of a lap joint melt away easily. Sheet is often coated, oily or galvanised. A sheet WPS deals with these problems. It gives a small electrode, often 2.0 or 2.5 mm, and a low current range so that the heat input stays low. It may allow DCEN or vertical-down welding to keep the heat down. It sets a tight fit-up with a small root gap, close tacks and sometimes a backing bar. It gives the weld size, stitch lengths and sequence to control distortion, and it says how the sheet must be cleaned. It also lists the thickness range and positions it covers, so the welder knows the limits.
markingPoints: Names the problems: burn-through, distortion, edge melt-back, coatings
Small electrode and low current to keep heat input down
Fit-up controls: small gap, close tacks, backing bar
Sequence and stitch welds to control distortion
WPS states the thickness range, positions and cleaning

essays.stem: Describe how you would set up and weld a square butt joint in 2 mm sheet in the flat position to a WPS, including fit-up, backing, settings and sequence.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the WPS and check the electrode class and size, the current range and the root gap. I measure the sheet to confirm it is 2 mm. I clean the edges and both faces back about 25 mm to bright metal. I set the edges close together with the small gap the WPS allows, and clamp them over a copper or steel backing bar. I tack at both ends and then about every 50 mm, working from the middle out. I set the current low in the range and check it on scrap of the same sheet. I weld with a short arc and a steady, quite fast travel, with no weave. On a long seam I weld short runs in a skip or back-step order so the heat is spread. I fill each crater, clean the slag and check for full fusion, burn-through and flatness.
markingPoints: Reads the WPS and checks material thickness
Cleans edges and sets a close fit-up over a backing bar
Tacks closely, working from the middle out
Low current tested on scrap, short arc, steady travel
Uses a skip or back-step sequence and checks the result

essays.stem: Explain how arc spot (puddle) welds are made on steel roof deck and how they are checked. Include the safety controls for working on the deck.
essays.modelAnswer: An arc spot weld joins the deck to the steel beam under it. The welder holds the electrode upright on the deck at the marked spot, strikes the arc and burns through the top sheet, then moves the electrode in a small circle to build up a round weld that fuses into the beam below. The deck must sit tight on the beam, and if the sheet is very thin a weld washer may be used. The WPS gives the electrode, current and the size of the visible weld. Each weld is checked by eye for size, full fusion round its edge and no cracks. Test pieces are welded first and peel tested. On the deck, the area must have edge protection or harnesses, the deck must be fixed so it cannot slide, and galvanised deck needs fume control. Cables are kept tidy so no one trips, and a fire watch is kept.
markingPoints: Deck tight on the beam; burns through the top sheet with no hole first
Electrode upright, small circle to build a round weld fused to the beam
Weld size and settings from the WPS; washer for very thin deck
Checks: visual size and fusion, peel tests on trial pieces
Safety: fall protection, fume control on zinc, trip and fire controls

essays.stem: Compare lap, tee, corner and flare-bevel joints in sheet work. Say where each is used and the main point to watch when welding each one.
essays.modelAnswer: A lap joint has one sheet over another. It is used for panels and covers because it is easy to fit. The welder must not melt away the top edge, or the throat is lost. A tee joint has one sheet standing on another, as with stiffeners and brackets. The arc should favour the thicker part so the thin one does not burn back. A corner joint joins two sheets at an angle, as on boxes and cabinets. An open corner is easy to burn through, so a closed or half-open corner and a low current are used. A flare-bevel joint is made where the rounded corner of a bent section meets a flat sheet, as on purlins and tubes. The welder must get fusion into the bottom of the curved groove and fill it to the size given, without burning through the thin bend.
markingPoints: Lap: where used; protect the top edge and throat
Tee: where used; favour the thicker part
Corner: where used; burn-through risk, fit-up choice
Flare-bevel: rounded corner to flat; fuse the root of the groove
Clear comparison across all four joints

essays.stem: Explain why welded sheet panels distort, and describe five ways to control the distortion.
essays.modelAnswer: When a weld is made, the metal next to it expands with the heat and then shrinks as it cools. Thin sheet is not stiff enough to resist this shrinking force, so it bends, bows or buckles. The more heat put in, the worse the distortion. To control it, first keep the heat input low: a small electrode, low current and quick travel. Second, make the welds no bigger than the drawing asks, and use stitch welds where they are allowed. Third, clamp the sheet to a flat bench or jig, with backing bars, until it cools. Fourth, use a welding sequence such as back-step or skip welding, and balance welds on each side of the panel. Fifth, tack closely and evenly before welding. Bent edges or swages in the panel also add stiffness.
markingPoints: Explains expansion and shrinkage as the cause
Low heat input and correct weld size
Clamping, jigs and backing bars
Sequence: back-step, skip, balanced welding
Close, even tacking or other valid method

essays.stem: Describe how you would weld sheet in the vertical (3F or 3G) and overhead (4F) positions, and how the technique differs from flat welding.
essays.modelAnswer: In all positions on sheet I use a small electrode and a short arc. In the vertical position the WPS may allow vertical-down welding on thin sheet. I set the current a little lower than for flat, point the electrode slightly upward, and travel quickly so the pool stays small and the heat does not build up. If the WPS calls for vertical-up, I use small runs with a slight pause at the edges and no wide weave. Overhead, gravity pulls the pool down, so I use less current again, keep the arc very short and lay small, quick stringer runs. I stand to the side, out from under the pool, with a cap and collar buttoned. In the flat position the pool is held up by the sheet, so a steadier, slightly hotter run can be used. In each position I check fusion and look for burn-through and sagging.
markingPoints: Vertical: lower current, down where the WPS allows, fast travel
Vertical-up option: small runs, no wide weave
Overhead: lower current, very short arc, small stringers
Overhead body position and PPE
Compares with flat and names checks

essays.stem: Explain how a welder qualification test on low carbon steel sheet is carried out and assessed under the AWS code the Centre uses.
essays.modelAnswer: The test is set by the assessor from a qualified WPS. The welder is given the sheet of the stated thickness, the electrodes and the position, for example a butt joint in the vertical position or a fillet weld in a lap joint overhead. He must work to the WPS settings while the assessor watches. When it is finished the test piece is marked with his number. It is first checked by eye for size, cracks, undercut, burn-through and full fusion. Then test pieces are cut from the places the code sets out. Butt welds are bent round a former, and lap or spot welds are peeled or broken open to check fusion. The results go on the welder qualification record, which states the process, thickness range and positions he is now qualified for. The welder must keep using the process for the qualification to stay current.
markingPoints: Works from a qualified WPS with given sheet, electrode and position
Watched by the assessor; test piece identified
Visual inspection first
Bend, peel or break tests cut from set places
Results recorded on the WPQ with the range covered and how it stays current

essays.stem: Describe the hazards of arc welding galvanised and coated sheet, and the controls you would use.
essays.modelAnswer: Galvanised sheet has a zinc coating. When it is welded the zinc burns off as white fume. Breathing it can cause metal fume fever, with shivering, fever and aches some hours later. Painted or oily sheet can give off harmful smoke and gases too. The coating can also cause porosity and spatter. To control this, I first check what the coating is from the job papers or data sheet. Where the WPS allows, I grind the coating back from the weld area with dust controls. I weld with local fume extraction placed close to the arc, in a well-ventilated area, and wear a respirator suitable for metal fume if the extraction is not enough. I keep my head out of the plume. After welding I repair the coating with zinc-rich paint as the job asks. Anyone who feels unwell is reported and given first aid.
markingPoints: Names zinc fume and metal fume fever; other coatings give harmful fumes
Checks the coating type first
Removes coating where allowed, with dust control
Local extraction, ventilation and suitable respirator; head out of the plume
Repairs coating after; reports illness

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect a batch of welded sheet steel cabinets, which defects you would look for, and how you would record and report them.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with the drawing and the WPS so I know the weld sizes, stitch lengths and tolerances. Each cabinet is checked when the slag is removed and it is cool. I check the overall sizes, squareness by the diagonals, and flatness of the panels with a straight edge. I then look at every weld in good light. I look for burn-through, cracks, craters, undercut, edges melted back on lap joints, porosity, missing or short stitches, and spatter. I measure some fillet sizes with a gauge. Each cabinet gets a number, and the results go on an inspection sheet with pass or fail for each check. Faults are marked on the job in paint and written on a non-conformance note. I tell the supervisor, agree the repair, and check the cabinet again after the repair before it is passed.
markingPoints: Uses drawing and WPS for the acceptance limits
Checks sizes, squareness and flatness
Names sheet weld defects to look for
Records results per numbered cabinet on an inspection sheet
Marks faults, reports, and re-inspects repairs

essays.stem: As team leader, explain how you would plan, run and check a job to weld 30 sheet steel machine guard panels for a factory in Spanish Town.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the drawings and the WPS, and list the sheet, angle, electrodes and consumables needed. I would check that each welder is qualified for the sheet thickness and positions. I would plan the work in stages: cutting and fit-up, tacking in a jig, welding, cleaning and inspection. I would make a simple jig so every panel is the same. Before production, one panel is welded to the WPS and checked for size, weld quality and flatness. If it passes, it becomes the sample. I would give each person a clear task and agree a daily target. During the job I would check the current settings, watch the welding sequence and keep the area safe and tidy. Each finished panel is inspected and recorded. At the end I would write a short report on the quantity, faults found and lessons learned.
markingPoints: Reads drawings and WPS; lists materials
Checks welder qualifications
Plans stages and uses a jig
First-off trial panel checked before production
Supervises, inspects each panel and reports

practical1.title: Butt and lap joints in 2 mm sheet to a WPS, flat and vertical-down, with bend and break checks
practical1.brief: Your group is given a sheet steel WPS by the assessor. As a group, read it and write the settings on a weld record sheet. Each member then welds two test pieces in 2 mm low carbon steel sheet: a square butt joint in the flat position (1G) over a backing bar, and a lap joint fillet weld in the vertical position welded downward (3F), if the WPS allows it. Each member sets the current, tacks, welds, fills craters and cleans their own pieces. One member acts as inspector for each round (take turns), checking another member's welds by eye against the WPS and recording the result. The assessor then cuts strips from the butt joints for bend tests on the Centre's bend tester and the group breaks open the lap joints in a vice. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the weld record sheet once for the whole group.
materials: Low carbon steel sheet, 2 mm thick, cut to about 150 mm × 50 mm (4 pieces per member)
2.0 mm or 2.5 mm E6013 electrodes, as the WPS gives
Copper or steel backing bar and clamps
Sheet steel WPS and blank weld record sheet (from the assessor)
Caliper, straight edge and fillet gauge
Bend tester or former and a vice
photos: The WPS and the completed weld record sheet
Each member's butt joint tacked over the backing bar
Finished butt welds, face and back
Broken lap joints showing the fusion
checklist: Read the WPS and set the current within its range, tested on scrap
Measured the sheet thickness and cleaned the edges before fit-up
Tacked closely and fitted the butt joint over the backing bar
Kept a short arc and steady travel with no burn-through
Filled craters and cleaned the slag from each run
Inspected another member's weld against the WPS and recorded it correctly
Wore full PPE and kept the booth safe and tidy
safety: Weld only in a booth or behind screens, with fume extraction on
Treat all sheet as hot after welding: use tongs and mark it HOT
Thin sheet edges are sharp: wear gloves when handling
Keep gloves and clothing dry; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules for the machine

practical2.title: Sheet panel fixed to an angle frame with arc spot and stitch welds, with peel tests and a flatness check
practical2.brief: As a group, make a small test panel like a section of steel deck: a sheet of 1.5–2 mm low carbon steel, about 600 mm × 400 mm, fixed to a frame of 40 mm × 40 mm angle that the assessor provides already welded. First write a short plan: the welding sequence, where each arc spot weld goes (mark a grid), and the stitch weld lengths and spacing from the assessor's drawing. Clamp the sheet tight to the frame. Each member makes at least three arc spot welds and one stitch weld, following the plan's sequence. Before welding the panel, each member makes two arc spot welds on a small lapped test piece, and the group peel tests them to show the weld pulls out a button. When the panel is finished, check its flatness with a straight edge at marked points and record the readings. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the plan and the readings once for the whole group.
materials: Low carbon steel sheet, 1.5–2 mm, about 600 mm × 400 mm
Welded 40 mm × 40 mm angle frame (from the assessor)
Small sheet and flat bar offcuts for peel test pieces
2.5 mm E6013 electrodes, or as the assessor's WPS gives
G-clamps, straight edge, feeler gauges or a rule, soapstone or paint marker
Assessor's drawing and blank plan sheet
photos: The written plan with the marked grid and sequence
The sheet clamped to the frame before welding
Peel test pieces after pulling apart, showing the buttons
Arc spot welds on the panel, close up
The finished panel with stitch welds
Flatness check with the straight edge and the recorded readings
checklist: Helped write a plan with a sensible sequence and weld positions
Clamped the sheet tight to the frame before welding
Made sound arc spot welds of even size, fused round their edges
Made a stitch weld to the length and spacing on the drawing
Peel tested a test piece and judged the result correctly
Worked safely and left the area clean, with stubs in a metal bin
safety: Use fume extraction; if any sheet is galvanised, extraction and a suitable respirator are a must
Keep the welding cable and work lead tidy so no one trips
Use pliers or a vice for peel tests; wear safety glasses
Hot panels stay on the bench and are marked HOT until cool
